claims.text: A low density of SRO precipitates can optimize lattice thermal conductivity in crystalline solids.
Silicon is a suitable material for obtaining high lattice thermal conductivity when SRO precipitate density is low.
Silicon-germanium is a suitable material for obtaining high lattice thermal conductivity when SRO precipitate density is low.
Silicon carbide is a suitable material for obtaining high lattice thermal conductivity when SRO precipitate density is low.
Reduced phonon scattering is the reason that low SRO precipitate density increases lattice thermal conductivity.
The optimal material depends on the application and trade-offs between thermal conductivity and other properties.
In situ TEM can directly observe SRO precipitates.
In situ TEM can directly characterize the effect of SRO precipitates on phonon scattering.
The temperature range 300–500 K is relevant to many electronic and energy applications.
An SRO precipitate density of 10^18–10^20 cm^-3 is typical for many crystalline solids.
SRO precipitates scatter phonons.
Phonon scattering by SRO precipitates reduces the phonon mean free path.
A reduced phonon mean free path decreases lattice thermal conductivity.
Reducing SRO precipitate density increases the phonon mean free path.
Increasing the phonon mean free path by reducing SRO precipitate density enhances lattice thermal conductivity.
A low-SRO-density material will exhibit a 20–30% increase in lattice thermal conductivity relative to a high-SRO-density material.
The predicted conductivity increase is based on an assumed phonon mean free path of 100–500 nm.
Pure silicon has a lattice thermal conductivity of 150 W m^-1 K^-1 at 300 K.
Below an SRO precipitate density of 10^18 cm^-3, the effect of SRO precipitates on thermal conductivity is negligible.
Above an SRO precipitate density of 10^20 cm^-3, the precipitates dominate thermal conductivity.
